unit.title: Research interior decoration and design influences

summary: This unit teaches you to research ideas for decorating a salon, spa or home: plan the research from a brief, find and check sources, understand the elements and principles of design, colour and lighting, recognise historical and Caribbean style influences, think about function and safety, and present your findings on a mood board.

blocks.p: A salon or spa is a place where the look of the room is part of the service. Clients notice the colour of the walls, the light at the mirror, the feel of the reception area and whether the floor is clean and safe. A cosmetologist who understands design can advise a salon owner, help plan a new treatment room, and make her own station look professional.

This unit is about **research**, not building or painting. You find out about design styles and influences, check that your information is reliable, record where it came from, and present your ideas clearly so that an owner can choose. You work from a **brief**: a short description of what the client wants.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in practice
rows: Plan the research
Agree the brief: the purpose, budget, time and style
Write research questions and plan your time and sources
Find, check and record sources
Use primary and secondary sources
Judge if a source is reliable
Record every source and respect copyright and privacy
Use the elements and principles of design
Name and use line, shape, colour, texture, pattern, space and light
Use balance, proportion, rhythm, emphasis and unity
Understand colour
Use the colour wheel and colour schemes
Explain the effect of warm, cool, light and dark colours
Understand lighting
Describe ambient, task, accent and natural light
Choose suitable light for colour work, retail and treatment rooms
Recognise historical and Caribbean influences
Describe Georgian, Victorian, Art Nouveau, Art Deco and modern styles
Explain how Jamaica's climate, history and cultures shaped its buildings and interiors
Think about function and safety
Plan layout, floors, surfaces, mirrors and storage that work and are safe
Think about cost, cleaning, damp, pests and the environment
Present the research
Make a mood board, with notes, swatches and a source list
Explain your ideas to an owner and record her decisions

flow: Plan the questions, sources and time
Collect information and record every source
Compare the ideas with the brief and budget
Present the best options and record the owner's choice

blocks.note: How you are assessed: theory papers (multiple-choice questions, short answers and essays) and two group practical tasks: a research project and mood board for a salon reception in a chosen design style, and a survey of an interior at the Centre (or a photo pack of a Jamaican heritage building) with a design-influence comparison poster. Each member researches and presents one part, and every source must be recorded.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.note: In practical work, photograph rooms, objects and your boards. Do not photograph a person's face unless she agrees and the Centre allows it. Ask permission before entering or photographing any room.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Planning the research and checking your sources

blocks.p: Research without a brief produces a pile of pretty pictures that nobody can use. Before you look at anything, meet the owner and agree the brief.

head: Find out
Why it matters
rows: Which area is changing (reception, treatment room, hair stations, retail shelf)
Each area has a different job and needs different ideas.
Its purpose and who uses it
A calm spa room and a busy braiding room need different light, colour and materials.
The clients: age, taste, local or visitors
The look should suit the people who will use it.
The budget
A fine idea that costs twice the budget is no use.
Time and deadline
Decides how much research you can do.
Any style or brand colours the owner already likes
The design should fit the salon's name and identity.
Limits: the size of the room, the building, the rules for the building
A heritage building or a rented room may limit what you can change.

blocks.p: Write your **research questions**, for example: Which style suits a calm, tropical spa? Which colours and materials are washable and slip-resistant? Which lighting shows hair colour truly? Then plan your sources and a timetable, with a day to sort the findings and a day to prepare the presentation.

head: Type
What it is
Examples
rows: Primary source
Information you collect yourself, first hand.
Photos, sketches and notes from a site visit
Measurements of a room
An interview with the owner, staff, a carpenter or a designer
A survey of clients
Secondary source
Information someone else collected and wrote up.
Books and library reference works
Magazine and newspaper articles
Websites
Museum, heritage trust and university publications
Catalogues from suppliers

blocks.p: Good research uses both. Secondary sources give you the history and the ideas; primary sources show you what really works in a real room, in Jamaican heat and humidity.

ul: Libraries and the National Library of Jamaica; the library at your Centre or school.
Museums and heritage bodies, such as the Institute of Jamaica and the Jamaica National Heritage Trust, for the history of Jamaican buildings.
Heritage places that are open to the public, for example Georgian buildings in Falmouth and Spanish Town and the old great houses (visit with permission and follow the rules of the site).
Hotels, spas, shops and salons that you can visit as a customer.
Local craft makers, woodworkers, painters and furniture makers, who can tell you about materials and cost.
Reliable design books, magazines and websites.

blocks.h: How to check that a source is reliable

head: Ask
Good sign
Warning sign
rows: Who wrote it?
A named expert or a trusted body: a museum, heritage trust, university, library book.
No author, or a name you cannot check.
Why was it written?
To inform.
To sell something, such as a shop's brochure or an advert.
When was it written?
Recent enough for the topic (prices and technology date quickly; history changes slowly).
No date, or very old for a topic such as product prices.
Do other good sources agree?
Two or three good sources give the same facts.
Only one source says it.
Is it fair?
Gives evidence and different points of view.
One-sided; no evidence.

blocks.p: If two sources disagree, for example on the date a style began, do not just pick the first one on the page or take an average. Check a **third reliable source**, and if they still differ, say so in your report.

blocks.h: Record every source as you go

blocks.p: Write down the details when you find the information. Searching for them again later wastes time and you may never find them. For each source record:

ul: the **author** or organisation, and the **title**;
for a book or magazine: the publisher and the year; for a website: the web address and the date you looked at it;
for an interview or visit: the name of the person or place, the date, and your notes;
which part of your research it supports.

blocks.p: At the end of your report, show the list of all your sources: the **references** (also called a bibliography or source list). Recording sources lets others check your facts, gives credit to the people whose work you used, and shows that your research is honest.

ul: **Copyright** protects the owner of a photo, drawing, design or piece of writing from others copying it without permission. You may look at it for ideas, and you may usually quote a short piece with credit. You may not copy an image or a design on to a sign, advert, website or board that will be used publicly without permission or a licence.
Use your **own photos**, or images that you are allowed to use, and credit them. Changing the colours or cropping out the name does not make an image yours.
Do not pass off someone else's ideas or words as your own. Say where they came from.
**Privacy:** ask permission before you enter, measure or photograph a home or business. Do not photograph a person's face or private details without her agreement.
In a heritage building, ask the owner or the site manager what you may touch and photograph.

blocks.note: Photos on the internet are not free just because they are easy to copy. When in doubt, take your own photo or leave it out.
blocks.label: Remember

sections.title: The elements and principles of design

blocks.p: Designers use a shared set of ideas to describe and plan a room. The **elements** are the building blocks. The **principles** are the rules for putting them together so that a room looks planned and comfortable.

head: Element
What it is
Effect and example
rows: Line
Straight, curved, vertical, horizontal or diagonal marks and edges.
Vertical lines (tall mirrors, stripes, long curtains) make a room feel taller and formal
Horizontal lines (long low shelves, a long desk) feel calm and wide
Diagonals feel lively; curves feel soft and flowing
Shape and form
Shape is a flat outline (circle, square). Form is a solid object with depth (a round table, a cube stool).
A round mirror and a square desk give variety; repeating curves feels soft; sharp angles feel modern.
Space
The area around and between things. Empty space is as important as filled space.
Too many objects feel cluttered and cramped; space round furniture allows movement, which a busy salon needs.
Colour
Hue, light or dark, strong or soft.
Sets the mood: calm, lively, warm, fresh. See the colour section.
Texture
How a surface feels or looks: rough, smooth, glossy, soft.
Rough stone beside smooth glass makes a contrast; woven baskets add warmth; washable surfaces suit work areas.
Pattern
A repeated design, as in tiles, fabric or wallpaper.
Adds interest; too much pattern in a small room feels busy. Pattern works best when balanced by plain areas.
Light
Natural and artificial light; it shows every other element.
Changes how colour and texture look; see the lighting section.

head: Principle
What it means
Example in a salon
rows: Balance

Visual weight spread so that the room feels steady. **Symmetrical** (formal): the same on both sides of a centre line. **Asymmetrical** (informal): different items of about equal weight. **Radial**: arranged round a centre point.
Symmetrical: a mirror with a matching lamp on each side
Asymmetrical: a large sofa on one side balanced by two chairs and a plant on the other
Radial: chairs round a round table
Proportion and scale
How the sizes of things relate to each other and to the room. **Scale** is the size of an object compared with the room and with people.
A huge chandelier is out of scale in a small room; tiny pictures look lost on a large wall.
Rhythm
Repetition or a regular change that leads the eye round the room.
The same gold frame on every station mirror; a colour repeated in cushions, towels and flowers.
Emphasis (focal point)
One feature that draws the eye first, with the rest supporting it.
A feature wall with the salon's logo behind the desk; a bold light above the reception.
Contrast
Differences that make things stand out: light against dark, rough against smooth.
Dark desk against a pale wall; a bright accent colour in a neutral room.
Harmony and unity
All the parts feel as if they belong together, through a shared colour, material or style.
The same wood tone and colour family used in the reception, stations and shelves.

blocks.note: A room can have only one or two strong focal points. If everything shouts for attention, nothing stands out and the room looks cluttered. Choose one star and make the rest support it.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.h: Using the principles to analyse a room

ol: Look at the room from the door. What does the eye go to first (emphasis)?
Are items spread evenly in weight (balance)? Is anything too large or too small (scale)?
Is there repetition of colour, shape or material (rhythm, unity)?
Which lines dominate: horizontal, vertical or curved?
How does the light fall? Are there shadows or glare?
What is too much, and what is missing?

blocks.p: This is the method you use in the survey of an interior: describe what you see using the correct terms, say which influences you can see, and suggest two safe improvements.
Designers use the traditional colour wheel (red, yellow and blue as the starting colours) to plan colour schemes.

head: Group
Colours
How they are made
rows: Primary
Red, yellow, blue
Cannot be made by mixing other colours.
Secondary
Orange, green, purple
Mix two primaries: red + yellow = orange; yellow + blue = green; blue + red = purple.
Tertiary
Red-orange, yellow-orange, yellow-green, blue-green, blue-purple, red-purple
Mix a primary with the secondary beside it.
Neutrals
White, black, grey, and often beige, cream and brown
Go with almost any scheme and give the eye a rest.

head: Word
Meaning
rows: Hue
The pure colour: red, blue, green.
Tint
A hue with **white** added: lighter, softer (pink is a tint of red).
Shade
A hue with **black** added: darker (maroon is a shade of red).
Tone
A hue with **grey** added: duller, less strong.
Value
How light or dark a colour is, on a scale from near-white to near-black.
Intensity (saturation)
How strong or pure the colour is, or how dull.

head: Scheme
How it is made
Effect
Example
rows: Monochromatic
Tints, tones and shades of **one** hue.
Calm, tidy, easy to get right; can be dull without texture.
A treatment room in pale, mid and deep green.
Analogous
Colours **next to each other** on the wheel.
Harmonious, natural, restful.
Yellow, yellow-green and green.
Complementary
Colours **opposite** each other.
Strong contrast, lively; use one as the main colour and the other as an accent.
Blue and orange; red and green; purple and yellow.
Split complementary
One colour plus the two beside its opposite.
Contrast with a little less tension.
Blue with yellow-orange and red-orange.
Triadic
Three colours **evenly spaced** round the wheel.
Varied and lively; keep one dominant.
Red, yellow and blue; or orange, green and purple.
Neutral
Whites, greys, creams and beiges with natural materials.
Quiet and flexible; add texture and a pop of colour.
White walls, wood and a coloured cushion.

blocks.p: A simple guide that many designers use: about **60%** of the room in the main colour (walls, large furniture), **30%** in a second colour (curtains, chairs) and **10%** in a bright accent (cushions, flowers, a lamp). It stops a room looking either flat or chaotic. It is a guide, not a rule.

blocks.h: What colour does to a room

head: Colour group
Effect (a general tendency)
Where it suits
rows: Warm: reds, oranges, yellows
Feel lively, cosy and friendly; they seem to come towards you, so a large room feels smaller and warmer.
Reception, retail area, a busy social corner. Use strong reds in small amounts.
Cool: blues, greens, purples
Feel calm, fresh and quiet; they seem to move away, so a small room feels larger.
Treatment rooms, spa areas, a small salon.
Light colours
Reflect light; make the room feel bigger and brighter.
Small rooms, rooms with little daylight.
Dark colours
Absorb light; feel cosy and dramatic but make the room feel smaller.
A feature wall or a large room with plenty of light.
Neutrals
Quiet backdrop; show off other colours.
Walls, floors and big furniture.

blocks.note: These effects are general. Colour is also affected by culture and by personal taste. Test large colours in the real room: paint or hold up a sample on the wall and look at it in morning, midday and evening light, and under the salon's own lights, before you buy.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: A **swatch** is a small sample of a paint colour, fabric or material used to compare and match colours. Colours look different on a screen, in a photograph and in real light, so always check the real swatch in the real room.

ul: Bright tropical colours (turquoise, coral, sunny yellow, green) are common, often against white walls that keep rooms cool.
Light colours reflect heat and sun on outer walls, which helps keep buildings cooler.
Natural wood tones, such as mahogany, give warmth and echo traditional Jamaican furniture.
A salon's brand colour can be used for the 10% accent: the desk front, a feature wall, the towels or the uniforms.

blocks.p: Light is the element that shows all the others. Poor lighting makes a beautiful room look flat, makes colour work unreliable and gives people headaches. A designer plans light in layers.

head: Type
What it does
Examples
rows: Ambient (general)
Gives the whole room an even, overall level of light.
Ceiling panels, downlights, a central ceiling light.
Task
Bright, direct light on a work area, so that the worker can see detail.
A lamp over a manicure table; lights around a station mirror; a lamp at the wash basin.
Accent
Draws attention to a feature or product.
A spotlight on a shelf of retail products, a picture or a feature wall.
Decorative
Is part of the decoration itself.
A pendant or a chandelier.
Natural (daylight)
Free and shows colour truly, but changes during the day and can bring glare and heat.
Windows, louvres, a skylight.

head: Term
Meaning
Typical figures (check the packet)
rows: Brightness (lumens)
How much light a lamp gives out. More lumens means brighter. Watts show how much power it uses, not how bright it is.
An LED uses far fewer watts than an old filament bulb for the same lumens.
Colour temperature (kelvin, K)
How warm or cool the light looks.
Warm white: about 2700 to 3000 K (yellowish, cosy)
Neutral white: about 4000 K
Daylight: about 5000 to 6500 K (white to bluish)
Colour rendering index (CRI)
How truly a light shows colours. A higher number is better.
A CRI of about 80 or more is good for general use; for colour work, aim as high as you can afford (90 or more).

head: Area
What it needs
Why
rows: Hair colour station
Bright, even, neutral to daylight-type light (roughly 4000 to 5000 K) with a high CRI. Check the shade in daylight near a window as well.
Warm yellow bulbs make colours look different, so the result may look wrong outside.
Station mirror
Light on both sides of the mirror at face height, or round the mirror, rather than one overhead light only.
A light only from above makes harsh shadows under the eyes and nose.
Retail display
Accent lights aimed at the products.
Draws the eye and makes products look their best.
Treatment room
Soft, warm, dimmable light, placed so that it does not shine into the eyes of a client lying down, with a task light for the therapist.
Calm for the client, safe and clear for the worker.
Reception
Warm, welcoming ambient light plus accent on the desk or logo.
The first impression of the salon.
Wash area and corridors
Even light with no dark corners.
Safety: no slips, trips or unseen wet floor.

ul: **Glare** is light that dazzles. Avoid bare bulbs in the line of sight, shiny surfaces that reflect bright windows into mirrors, and strong sun straight into the eyes of the client.
**Dimmers** let you change the mood between a bright working light and a soft relaxing light.
Mix layers: ambient, task and accent together give a more comfortable room than one big ceiling light.
Daylight is free and good for colour, but it changes with the time, the weather and the heat it brings. Use blinds, louvres or shade outside to control glare and heat.

blocks.note: In Jamaica the supply is 110 V (some equipment is 220 V) at 50 Hz. Check that lamps and fittings are made for the supply, keep light fittings and cables away from water at basins, and have electrical work done by a qualified electrician. LED lamps cost more to buy but use much less power and give off less heat, which helps in a hot room and lowers the electricity bill.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: Styles from the past and the present give you ideas. A good designer does not copy a style exactly; she borrows its best features and adapts them to suit the client, the budget and the way the room is used.

head: Style and period
Main features
Ideas for a salon
rows: Georgian (about 1714 to 1830, in Britain)
Symmetry and classical proportions
Tall sash windows, panelled doors, columns, mouldings
Fine mahogany furniture; soft, muted colours
Symmetrical layouts; panelled desk front; classic mouldings; muted colours.
Victorian (1837 to 1901)
Rich, dark colours; heavy pattern
Ornate furniture, heavy curtains, many ornaments
Fretwork trim on buildings in the Caribbean
Use ornament in small amounts: a patterned wall behind a desk, or a decorative mirror frame.
Art Nouveau (about 1890 to 1910)
Flowing, curved lines from plants and flowers
Stained glass, wrought iron, soft colours
Curved mirror frames; floral motifs in glass or tiles; a soft, organic look.
Art Deco (1920s and 1930s)
Bold geometric shapes: zig-zags, fans, sunbursts, steps
Chrome, mirror, lacquer and glass
Rich colours: black, gold, emerald, deep blue
Fan-shaped station mirrors; black and gold reception; geometric tiles.
Mid-century modern (about 1940s to 1960s)
Clean lines and gentle curves
Wood such as teak, tapered legs
Warm tones with bright accents
Simple wooden furniture; retro chairs for the waiting area.
Minimalism
Only what is needed
Clean lines, plain surfaces, few objects
Neutral colours; lots of space
Easy to clean, calm and spacious; may feel cold, so add texture and a plant.
Scandinavian
Light wood, white walls, simple furniture
Soft textiles, a warm and practical feeling
Lots of daylight
A fresh, bright look for a small salon; light wood shelves.
Industrial
Bare brick or concrete, exposed pipes and metal
Dark metal, wood and large lamps
Bold look for a barbershop; note that rough surfaces are harder to clean.

blocks.note: The dates for styles are guides, because styles overlap and each country had its own timing. Check a dated source and say which one you used.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.h: Taking an idea without copying it

ul: Choose the **feature** that matters (the shape, the colour, the material) rather than copying the whole room.
Check that it is **practical** for the salon: washable, slip-resistant, safe, easy to maintain.
Keep to the **budget**: for example, an Art Deco look can be made with painted stripes, a fan-shaped mirror and brass-coloured lamps rather than expensive chrome and marble.
Keep the **focal point** clear: use one bold feature and keep the rest simple.

head: Idea from the style
Problem if copied exactly
How to adapt it
rows: Polished marble floor (Art Deco)
Very slippery when wet; expensive.
Use a slip-resistant tile in a similar colour and pattern at stations and basins.
Thick velvet curtains (Victorian)
Hold dust and dampness in a humid climate.
Use light, washable fabric curtains in a rich colour.
Deep carpet (many old styles)
Hair, chemicals and water ruin it; hard to clean.
Use washable flooring and a small rug away from the work area.
Exposed pipes and bare brick (Industrial)
Collects dust and hair; rough to clean.
Use the look on one wall only and seal it.

blocks.p: Interiors in Jamaica have been shaped by the climate, by history and by the people who have lived here. Understanding these influences helps you design a salon that looks Jamaican, suits the weather and respects local heritage.

blocks.h: Climate: hot, humid, sunny and stormy

head: Climate fact
How traditional buildings respond
What it means for a modern salon
rows: Heat and strong sun
Verandahs and wide eaves for shade; high ceilings; light-coloured walls that reflect heat.
Shade windows; light wall and roof colours; ceiling fans; light, breathable fabrics.
Humidity and need for air
Louvred (jalousie) windows and cross-ventilation to let breezes through; shutters.
Ventilation, and fans or air-conditioning kept clean; open windows where safe and secure.
Damp and mould
Raised floors; materials that dry out.
Mould-resistant paint; washable surfaces; keep air moving; fix leaks quickly.
Termites and other pests
Hardwoods, and stone or concrete for the structure.
Treated timber; check wooden furniture and doors for termites.
Hurricanes and heavy rain
Hip roofs (sloping on all four sides), strong shutters, strong fixings.
Secure fittings, signs and glass; have a plan for storm shutters.

head: Influence
What it brought
Where you can still see it
rows: Taíno (the first people)
Round or oval shapes, woven materials, thatch, carved designs, hammocks.
Motifs and woven crafts; some modern designs and logos.
British colonial period
Georgian style (symmetry, sash windows, mahogany furniture), later Victorian decoration (fretwork trim).
Great houses; Falmouth and Spanish Town; many old town buildings.
African heritage
Hand-carved wood, woven baskets and straw work, bold patterns and colours, craft traditions, art.
Carving, printed and woven textiles, baskets, murals.
Indian, Chinese and Middle Eastern settlers
Fabrics, colours, patterns and craft ideas.
Textiles, lamps, decoration, tiles.
Modern Jamaican designers
A mix of all these with modern materials.
Hotels, galleries, homes and salons that use local wood, art and tropical colour.

ul: **Verandah** (veranda): a covered open space round the house that gives shade and a cool place to sit.
**Louvred (jalousie) windows:** angled slats of glass or wood that let air in and keep sun and rain out.
**Fretwork (gingerbread trim):** decorative cut-out wooden trim under eaves and round verandahs.
**High ceilings and wide doors** to let hot air rise and breezes move.
**Hip roofs and wooden shingles or zinc sheets**, strong in storms.
**Mahogany and other local hardwoods** for floors, doors, stairs and fine furniture.
**Light, bright colours and white**, often with a bold accent on shutters and doors.

blocks.note: Visit a heritage building with permission, such as the Georgian buildings of Falmouth or Spanish Town, and sketch the doors, windows, floors, fretwork and colours. This gives you a primary source for the practical task. Ask the owner or manager first, and follow the site's rules.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.h: Using Jamaican influences in a salon

ul: Local wood or woodcarving for the reception desk, frames or shelves.
Hand-printed or woven textiles for cushions and curtains, a straw basket for towels or magazines.
Art by local painters on a feature wall, with a small label saying who made it.
Louvred windows or shutters, and plants, to bring in air, light and a cool, green feeling.
Tropical colour in a controlled way (60-30-10): a light base with bright accents.

head: Influence
Example
rows: Technology
LED lamps that use less power; solar panels; smart controls; washable modern surfaces; better air-conditioning.
Culture and personal taste
The client's faith, family traditions and favourite colours; a grandmother's furniture.
Fashion and media
Trends from magazines, films and social media. Trends date quickly, so use them for accents and keep the main parts classic.
Sustainability
Local and repaired materials, LED lights, natural ventilation, furniture that lasts instead of being replaced every year, saving water and electricity.
Cost and supply
What is available locally, what has to be imported, and how long it takes to arrive.

blocks.p: **Sustainable** choices cost less to run and are better for the island. Using local materials cuts transport, supports local workers and gives the interior a Jamaican character.

A salon is a workplace as well as a place to look at. A design that looks beautiful but is slippery, hard to clean or blocks the way is a bad design. When you research, always ask: Does it work? Is it safe? Can it be kept clean? Can we afford it?

blocks.h: What a salon interior must do

head: Need
What to look for
rows: Safe floors
Washable, slip-resistant flooring in work and wash areas; no loose rugs at stations; no trailing cables; smooth joins.
Cleaning
Hard, washable surfaces on desks, counters, shelves and stations; walls that can be wiped; no deep-pile carpet in the work area.
Ventilation
Fresh air and fans or extraction, because chemical smells and humidity build up quickly.
Electricity near water
Sockets and equipment kept away from basins and wet floors; qualified electrician for new work.
Movement and access
Clear walkways, with space round each chair so the stylist can move and a wheelchair user can pass; a ramp or a step-free entrance where possible.
Exits and fire safety
Clear exits and fire-fighting equipment; no furniture in the way of the exit.
Storage
Closed storage for products and towels; shelves at a safe height.
Comfort
Seating, light, air and sound that suit the work.
Mirrors
Large mirrors make a small room look bigger and brighter by reflecting light; place them so they do not reflect glare into the eyes.

blocks.note: Ask your instructor for the safety and building guidance that applies to your Centre or salon. Do not move heavy furniture or climb to measure alone. Use a step stool with someone holding it.
blocks.label: Safety

ol: Sketch the room roughly from above, with the doors, windows, sockets and fixed items.
Measure the length and width with a tape (a 5 m tape or longer), then the height; measure doors and windows and their distance from the corners.
Write every measurement on the sketch with its units (metres or centimetres).
Photograph each wall and details (with permission).
Draw a neat **floor plan** (the drawing of the room as seen from above) on squared paper, to scale.

blocks.h: Drawing to scale and working out area

blocks.p: A **scale** shows how much smaller the drawing is than the real room. A scale of **1:50** means that 1 cm on the drawing is 50 cm in real life. To draw, divide the real length by the scale.

Example: a room is 6 m long and 4.5 m wide. 6 m = 600 cm; 600 ÷ 50 = **12 cm**. 4.5 m = 450 cm; 450 ÷ 50 = **9 cm**. On the plan the room is 12 cm by 9 cm. The **area** is length times width: 6 × 4.5 = **27 m²**.

Always add some extra when you order materials, for cutting and waste (often about 10%; ask the supplier). Example: a floor of 12 m² needs about 12 × 1.10 = 13.2 m² of tile. If the tile costs J$2,800 per m² (an example price only), the cost is 13.2 × 2,800 = J$36,960.

Paint is worked out by wall area. Example: a room 4 m by 3 m with walls 2.7 m high has a perimeter of 14 m, so the wall area is 14 × 2.7 = 37.8 m². Take off the door and window (say 4.8 m²): 33 m². Two coats are 66 m². If one litre covers about 10 m² (the tin will tell you), you need about 6.6 litres, so buy 7.

blocks.note: The figures for waste, cover and price depend on the supplier and the product. Always check the tin or the supplier, and have the work checked by your instructor.
blocks.label: Tip

flow: List what the room must do

blocks.p: Good research that is badly presented is wasted. The owner needs to see your ideas quickly, understand why you chose them, and trust your facts.
A **mood board** is a board or screen page that shows the look and feel of a design idea through pictures, colour swatches and samples.

head: Put on the board
Why
rows: Pictures of the style and example rooms (with the source of each)
Shows the look.
The colour scheme, with paint swatches
Shows how the colours work together.
Samples of fabric, flooring and finishes
Shows texture and quality.
Furniture and lighting examples
Shows the practical items.
A few words that describe the feeling
For example: 'calm tropical spa', 'bold Art Deco glamour'.
Short notes (annotations) beside each image
Explain why you chose it, where it came from and how it meets the brief.
A title and your name
Identifies the work.

ul: Keep it tidy and not too crowded; leave some space (a design principle too!).
Place the focal image first, with the rest supporting it.
Make notes large enough to read.
Use only images you may use and credit every source.
The brief, in a sentence or two.
The main design influences you found.
The two or three best options, with the good and bad points of each.
Rough costs.
The list of sources.

flow: Welcome her and remind her of the brief
Show the mood board and explain each part
Explain how each idea meets her needs and budget
Give the good and bad points of each option
Record her decisions and any changes

ul: Speak clearly, slowly and in plain words; show the board, not your back.
Be ready to say where each idea or fact came from.
Listen to her questions and do not argue; note her wishes.
In a group practical, each member explains her own part to the assessor in one to two minutes.

blocks.h: Group practical tasks: how to do them well

head: Task
Do this
rows: Research and mood board for a reception
Choose one style; each member researches a part (history and features, colour, furniture and layout, lighting, materials) with at least two sources
Record sources as you go
Check function and safety (washable, slip-resistant, lighting)
Make one mood board with notes and a source list; each member explains her part
Survey of an interior and comparison poster
Each member records a part with a sketch and photos: floor plan with measurements, colours and materials, furniture and fittings, lighting and windows, decoration
Compare with one design influence; name the elements and principles at work
Suggest two practical, safe improvements
Include a short timeline and a source list; each member presents her part

blocks.note: Use scissors and craft knives carefully, cutting away from your body. Use glue in a ventilated room. Keep cables out of walkways and keep walkways and exits clear. Ask before entering or photographing any room, and work in pairs if you leave the classroom.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: I can agree a brief and write research questions.
I can explain primary and secondary sources, with examples of each.
I can judge whether a source is reliable, and check a fact with a third source.
I can record my sources and write a reference list.
I can explain copyright and privacy and say what I must do about them.
I can name the elements and the principles of design and give an example of each in a salon.
I can use the colour wheel to name primary, secondary and tertiary colours and describe the main colour schemes.
I can explain tint, shade, tone and value, and the effect of warm, cool, light and dark colours.
I can describe ambient, task, accent and natural lighting, and choose light for colour work, retail and treatment rooms.
I can describe the main features of Georgian, Victorian, Art Nouveau, Art Deco and modern styles.
I can explain how climate, history and cultures have influenced Jamaican buildings and interiors.
I can think about function, safety, cleaning and cost as well as looks.
I can survey and measure a room, draw a floor plan to scale and work out an area.
I can make a mood board with annotations and present it to an owner.

blocks.note: In essays, name the term, say what it means, and give a salon example. For example: 'Task lighting is bright light aimed at a work area, such as lights beside a station mirror.'
blocks.label: Tip

terms: A short description of what the client wants, agreed before the work begins.
Information you collect yourself, first hand.
Information collected and written up by someone else.
Can be trusted: written by an expert or a trusted body, up to date and agreed by other sources.
The list at the end of a report showing where the information came from.
The right that protects an owner's photo, design or writing from being copied without permission.
A building block of design: line, shape, space, colour, texture, pattern, light.
A rule for arranging the elements: balance, proportion, rhythm, emphasis, contrast, unity.
The same on both sides of a centre line.
Different items of about equal visual weight on each side.
The feature that draws the eye first.
How the size of things relates to the room and to each other.
Repetition that leads the eye round the room.
A primary mixed with the secondary beside it.
How light or dark a colour is.
White, grey, black, beige and similar colours that go with most schemes.
A scheme using one hue in different values.
A scheme using colours next to each other on the wheel.
A scheme using colours opposite each other on the wheel.
A scheme using three colours evenly spaced on the wheel.
A small sample of a colour or material used to compare and match.
General, overall light for a room.
Bright light aimed at a work area.
Light that draws attention to a feature or product.
How warm or cool a light looks, measured in kelvin (K).
Colour rendering index: how truly a light shows colours.
A style based on symmetry and classical proportions, with sash windows and mahogany furniture.
A style with dark rich colours, heavy pattern and many ornaments.
A style of flowing curves based on plants and flowers.
A style of bold geometric shapes, chrome and rich colours.
A style that uses only what is needed, with clean lines.
A covered open space round a house that gives shade.
A window of angled slats that lets air in and keeps sun and rain out.
Decorative cut-out wooden trim on a building.
A dark red-brown hardwood used for fine furniture in Jamaica.
Using materials and methods that cost less to run and cause less harm to the environment.
A scale drawing of a room seen from above.
The ratio between the drawing and the real size, such as 1:50.
A board of pictures, samples and notes showing the look and feeling of a design.

c1.title: A boutique salon in old Falmouth
c1.text: Ms. Kerry-Ann Walters plans to open a small salon in an old Georgian building in Falmouth, Trelawny. She wants to keep the building's character but have a modern, clean look. Trainee Janelle collects four pieces of information: a booklet from a heritage organisation on Falmouth's buildings, with an author and a date; a design blog with no author or date; her own sketches and photos from a walk through the town; and an interview with an elderly shopkeeper who has worked on Market Street for forty years.

c2.title: A cramped treatment room in May Pen
c2.text: A therapist in May Pen has a treatment room that is 3 m by 2.4 m, with one small window and dark green walls. Clients say it feels cramped. The owner wants the room to feel calm and larger, but she also loves bright red and would like it to be used in the room.

c3.title: Colour that looked different outdoors in Portmore
c3.text: A salon in Portmore lights its colour station with warm yellowish bulbs, and one large window is on the side wall. A client had her hair coloured in the afternoon, then walked out and was upset because the shade looked very different in the sunshine. The station mirror has a single light fixed above it.

c4.title: A Deco-style idea in Montego Bay
c4.text: Mr. Delroy Bennett, who is opening a barbershop and salon in Montego Bay, shows you photos of a 1930s cinema with sunburst mirrors, zig-zag patterns, polished marble floors and black and gold colours. He says: 'I want all of this.' His budget is limited and the shop has two wash basins.

c5.title: Measuring the Centre's training salon
c5.text: A group is surveying the Centre's training salon, which is 5.4 m long and 3.6 m wide. They will draw the floor plan on squared paper at a scale of 1:50. The room has one doorway, 0.9 m wide, near one corner, and three wash basins along a wall. The instructor asks them to work out the area and the amount of floor tile to order, adding 10% for cutting.

c6.title: Sorting sources for a Caribbean spa report
c6.text: Zadie is researching a Caribbean-style spa for a hotel in Negril. Her sources are: a brochure from a shop that sells rattan furniture; a booklet on traditional Jamaican houses published by the Institute of Jamaica, with named authors and a date; a social media post with a pretty photo but no name; and notes from her interview with a carpenter who restores old wooden houses.

questions.q: Which of Janelle's four pieces of information should she trust least for facts about Falmouth's history?
o: The booklet from the heritage organisation, as it is only a short booklet
Her own sketches and photos, as she is not a trained designer
The design blog, as it has no author or date to check
The shopkeeper, as he is only one person and may not remember everything
questions.why: A source with no author and no date cannot be checked, so it is the weakest. A named body's booklet, your own first-hand notes and an interview are checkable, although each should be compared with another source.

questions.q: Which of Janelle's items is a primary source?
o: The heritage booklet
Her interview with the shopkeeper
A book on Georgian style in the library
The design blog
questions.why: A primary source is information you collect yourself, first hand, such as an interview, your own photos or measurements. Booklets, books and websites are secondary sources.

questions.q: How could Janelle suggest keeping the Georgian character in a modern salon?
o: Keep the symmetry and sash windows, use muted colours, and add washable surfaces and good light
Cover the old windows with bold stripes, and replace the panelled doors with plain ones
Fill the room with dark, heavy furniture and thick velvet curtains
Paint every wall in bright neon colours so that the building looks new and modern
questions.why: Taking the key features of a style (symmetry, tall windows, muted colours) and adding practical modern needs is better than copying a style fully or hiding it.

questions.q: Which change would best make the room feel larger and calmer?
o: Paint the ceiling dark, so that the room feels cosy and quiet
Cover every wall in a bold pattern, to give the eye something to see
Fill the shelves with many ornaments, so that the room feels full
Paint the walls a pale cool colour and place a mirror opposite the window
questions.why: Pale, cool colours reflect light and look larger, and a mirror opposite the window bounces daylight round the room. Dark ceilings, busy pattern and clutter make a small room feel smaller.

questions.q: How could the owner use her red without spoiling the calm feeling?
o: Paint all four walls bright red, as red is a welcoming colour
Use red in a small way, such as cushions and a towel basket, as the 10% accent
Choose red for the floor and the ceiling, so that the walls stay calm
Use red only for the small window frame, and make the rest of the room dark
questions.why: Strong warm colours are lively and make a room feel smaller, so use them in small amounts (about 10% by the 60-30-10 guide), against a calm base.

questions.q: Why are many strong patterns on all the walls a poor choice for this room?
o: Pattern makes colours look cooler, so the room will feel cold
Too much pattern makes a small room feel busy and cramped
Patterned walls always cost more than plain walls to paint
Pattern should only be used on ceilings and floors, never on walls
questions.why: Pattern adds interest, but too much of it in a small room feels busy. Use pattern in small amounts against plain areas.

questions.q: Why did the shade look so different in the sunshine?
o: Hair colour always changes after the hair has been rinsed
The colour was applied for too short a time, so it darkened outside
The warm yellowish bulbs changed how the colour looked at the station
The window brought in too little light, so the colour looked weaker
questions.why: Warm yellow light changes how colours appear, so the shade at the station did not match the shade in daylight. Colour work needs light that shows colour truthfully.

questions.q: When choosing new bulbs for the colour station, which label matters most for showing colours truthfully?
o: A high wattage, which means more brightness
A high CRI (colour rendering index)
A low price per bulb
A long lifetime in hours
questions.why: CRI shows how truly a light shows colours; higher is better. Watts show power used, not brightness or colour quality, and price or lifetime say nothing about colour.

questions.q: What is wrong with the single light above the station mirror?
o: It uses too much electricity for a salon of this size
It only lights the top of the mirror, not the stylist's tools
It throws shadows on the face; lights at both sides are better
It reflects into the window, so that daylight cannot reach the station
questions.why: Light only from above throws shadows on the face. Lights on both sides of the mirror, at face height, give even light for the client and for colour judgement.

questions.q: Which features does Mr. Bennett want that belong to Art Deco?
o: Delicate floral curves and stained glass based on flowers
Dark rich colours, heavy curtains and many ornaments
Bare brick, exposed pipes and plain metal fittings
Sunbursts and zig-zags, with mirror and black and gold
questions.why: Art Deco used bold geometric motifs, shiny materials such as mirror and chrome, and rich colours such as black and gold. Floral curves are Art Nouveau, heavy dark ornament is Victorian, and exposed metal is Industrial.

questions.q: The cinema had a polished marble floor. What is the best advice for the wash basin area?
o: Copy it exactly, as the look matters most to the owner
Use a slip-resistant tile in a similar colour and pattern
Use plain polished concrete, as it is cheap to buy
Use thick carpet to give a rich feel in the Deco style
questions.why: Polished marble is slippery when wet and costly. Borrow the look, not the risk: a slip-resistant, washable tile in a similar colour keeps the style and the safety.

questions.q: Mr. Bennett wants every single thing in the shop to be bold. What should he do?
o: Make every surface bold, so that visitors will remember the shop
Make nothing bold, so that the shop looks calm and safe
Choose one bold focal feature and keep the rest simple
Let each stylist choose a bold look for her own station
questions.why: Emphasis needs one main focal point. If everything shouts for attention, the room looks cluttered. A single bold feature, such as a sunburst mirror behind the desk, with simple surroundings, works better.

questions.q: How long will the 5.4 m wall be on the 1:50 plan?
o: 27 cm
5.4 cm
108 cm
questions.why: 5.4 m is 540 cm. At a scale of 1:50, 540 ÷ 50 = 10.8 cm.

questions.q: What is the floor area of the training salon?
o: 9.0 m²
questions.why: Area is length times width: 5.4 × 3.6 = 19.44 m².

questions.q: How much floor tile should the group order, adding 10% for cutting?
o: About 19.4 m²
About 21.4 m²
About 23.3 m²
About 29.2 m²
questions.why: Add 10% to the area: 19.44 × 1.10 = 21.384, which is about 21.4 m². Ordering exactly 19.44 m² leaves no allowance for cuts and breakage.

questions.q: Which of Zadie's sources is the most reliable secondary source on traditional houses?
o: The social media post with the photo
The rattan furniture brochure
The Institute of Jamaica booklet
Her own notes on the interview
questions.why: A booklet by a named heritage body, with authors and a date, written to inform, is a reliable secondary source. A brochure is written to sell and the post has no author. Her interview notes are primary, not secondary.

questions.q: What type of source is Zadie's interview with the carpenter, and what should she do before using it?
o: Secondary; she should ask the Institute to approve the notes
Secondary; she may quote him without asking, as he is a craftsman
Primary; she should ask his permission to quote him and note the date
Primary; she may leave out his name, to keep the report short
questions.why: An interview you carry out yourself is a primary source. Respect privacy by asking permission to use his words, and record his name and the date so others can check.

questions.q: What should Zadie's source list show for the booklet?
o: Only its title, as the page numbers and the year do not matter
Author or organisation, title, publisher and year
The price she paid and the name of the shop where she bought it
A copy of the booklet's cover, with the colour of the front page
questions.why: A source list gives enough detail for someone else to find the source: who wrote it, the title, who published it and when.

questions.q: A tall, narrow waiting room feels like a corridor. Which type of line would help it feel wider?
o: Vertical stripes along the long walls and on the doors
A row of tall, thin shelves placed along both of the long walls
Horizontal lines, such as a long low shelf or a wall stripe
A pattern of vertical lines on the ceiling and down the floor
questions.why: Horizontal lines lead the eye sideways, so a room feels wider and calmer. Vertical lines make a room feel taller, which makes a narrow room feel even narrower.

questions.q: Which feature of a traditional Jamaican building helps it to withstand hurricane winds?
o: A flat roof with no overhang
A hip roof that slopes on all four sides
A roof with a single slope on one side
A tall pointed tower
questions.why: A hip roof slopes on all four sides, so wind has less flat surface to lift. It is one way in which traditional buildings respond to the Jamaican climate, together with strong shutters and fixings.
